1.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.
To translate the term **sons** here and through verse 8, see how you translated the similar expression in 8:12. Alternate translation: [descendants]

This phrase likely refers to military officers or royal officials who had been stationed in Jezreel but who had gone to Samaria for safety. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. The UST models one way to do that.

The author is using the possessive form to describe **guardians** whom **Ahab** had appointed to care for his children. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and to the guardians of Ahab’s children]

2.note: See how you translated this expression in 5:6, where it similarly occurs at the beginning of a letter.

Jehu is not referring to a specific **weapon**. He means weapons in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and weapons] or [and weaponry]

3.note: Jehu is using the adjectives **good** and **right** as nouns to mean a certain kind of person. The ULT indicates that by supplying the word **one**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the most capable and suitable person]

Jehu is using this son sitting **on the throne of his father** to represent him succeeding his father as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and you shall make him king as the successor to his father]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:18. Alternate translation: [the dynasty of your master]

4.note: The author is repeating the word **very** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [And they were extremely afraid] or [And they were terrified]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:9.

4.q: שְׁנֵ֣י הַ⁠מְּלָכִ֔ים לֹ֥א עָמְד֖וּ לְ⁠פָנָ֑י⁠ו וְ⁠אֵ֖יךְ נַעֲמֹ֥ד אֲנָֽחְנוּ
4.note: The officials are using the question form **how will we stand?** to emphasize that they cannot resist Jehu. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [Since two kings were not able to stand to his face, we certainly will not be able to stand!]

In this context, **stand** is a military term that means an army or soldier did not give way before an enemy. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You can also use plain language. Alternate translation: [could not hold their ground] or [did not survive]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:24. Alternate translation: [when they opposed him]

The leaders in Samaria are stating the pronoun **we** separately, even though the verb translated as **will we stand** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between these **kings**, who were experienced warriors commanding armies, and themselves as ordinary civilians. Alternate translation: [so how will we common people stand] or [so how will we common people be able to fight successfully against him]

5.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:13. Alternate translation: [Do what you consider to be good]

6.note: If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **second**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use. Alternate translation: [another letter]

Here, Jehu’s **voice** represents what he is saying by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you are listening to what I say]
See the discussion in the introduction to 2 Kings of how the author and characters often use the term “listen” to mean “agree.” Alternate translation: [and you agree to do what I say]

6.q: וּ⁠בְנֵ֤י הַ⁠מֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ שִׁבְעִ֣ים אִ֔ישׁ אֶת־גְּדֹלֵ֥י הָ⁠עִ֖יר מְגַדְּלִ֥ים אוֹתָֽ⁠ם
6.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

The author is using the adjective **great** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. The ULT indicates this by supplying the word **ones**. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase, here and in verse 11. Alternate translation: [the leading citizens of the city]

7.note: The author is speaking of this **letter** as if it had been a living thing that could have come to the leaders of Samaria on its own. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when they received the letter]
The pronoun **him** refers to Jehu. It may be helpful to use his name here in your translation. Alternate translation: [to Jehu]

9.note: The implication is that Jehu **stood** at the entrance of the city gate. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [and stood at the entrance of the city gate]

Jehu is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I conspired** already includes this meaning. He is doing that in order to emphasize a contrast between the people of Samaria, whom he calls **righteous**, and himself. Alternate translation: [I am guilty of conspiring against my master and killing him]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:23. Alternate translation: [But who killed all of these]

Jehu is using the question form for emphasis. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [But I did not kill all of these men!]

10.note: Jehu is speaking as if a **word** were a physical object that could fall **to the ground**. The image is that nothing Yahweh said **about the house of Ahab** has been lost or ruined, as happens to things that people drop or let fall. He means that everything Yahweh said has come true. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Samuel 3:19. Alternate translation: [has failed to come true]

It might seem that the expression **the word of Yahweh that Yahweh spoke** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you can shorten it. Alternate translation: [of what Yahweh said]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:18. Alternate translation: [the dynasty of Ahab]
See how you translated the similar expression in 9:36. Alternate translation: [through the agency of his servant Elijah]

11.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:23. Alternate translation: [And Jehu killed]
See how you translated the similar expression in 7:9. Alternate translation: [to the household of Ahab]

12.note: The author is saying **he arose and came** to describe something that was ongoing. This provides the background for an event he will describe that began to happen during this time. Connect this clause to the story in a way that makes it clear in your language that this clause is describing something that was ongoing in the background. Alternate translation: [Then Jehu began a journey to Samaria]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:24. Alternate translation: [And he took action]

13.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 9:21. Alternate translation: [and Jehu encountered]

As the parallel passage in 2 Chronicles 22:8 makes clear, these were not Ahaziah’s actual **brothers** but members of his extended family. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in the other instance of this phrase in this verse. Alternate translation: [family members of Ahaziah]
See how you translated the similar expression “go up” in 1:3. Alternate translation: [and we have come]

These relatives of Ahaziah are using the expression **for the welfare of** as a common expression of their culture to describe coming to visit family or friends with a particular interest in their health and well-being. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to see how the sons of the king and the sons of the queen mother are doing]

15.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 9:21. Alternate translation: [and he encountered]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [coming to meet him]

15.q: הֲ⁠יֵ֧שׁ אֶת־לְבָבְ⁠ךָ֣ יָשָׁ֗ר כַּ⁠אֲשֶׁ֤ר לְבָבִ⁠י֙ עִם־לְבָבֶ֔⁠ךָ
15.note: Here the **heart** represents a person’s feelings and commitments, in this case, loyalty. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Are you as prepared to be loyal to me as I am prepared to be loyal to you]

Giving his **hand** to Jehu (that is, shaking hands with him) was a symbolic action by which Jehonadab showed his agreement and alliance with Jehu. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [“If it is, shake hands with me to show we are allies.” And he shook hands with him]

This is a direct quotation from Jehu. If it would be helpful to your readers, introduce it as a direct quotation in a way that would be natural in your language. [And Jehu responded, “If it is, give your hand]

17.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 3:23. Alternate translation: [and he killed]
See how you translated the similar expression in 1:7. Alternate translation: [according to the message that Yahweh gave to Elijah]

18.q: אַחְאָ֕ב עָבַ֥ד אֶת־הַ⁠בַּ֖עַל מְעָ֑ט יֵה֖וּא יַעַבְדֶ֥⁠נּוּ הַרְבֵּֽה
18.note: When Jehu says that Ahab served Baal only a **little**, he is making an understatement in order to draw a comparison. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express this comparison. Alternate translation: [Compared to how much I am going to serve Baal, Ahab served him only a little]

Jehu is speaking of himself in the third person because he is making an authoritative proclamation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [I will serve him much]

The author is saying **all of the people** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [And Jehu called for a citywide meeting, and he said to the people]

19.note: The expressions **be missing** and **is missing** are passive verbal forms. If your language would not use these forms, you could express the idea they convey in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Let no man fail to attend … Everyone who fails to attend]

19.q: אִ֣ישׁ אַל־יִפָּקֵ֗ד כִּי֩ זֶ֨בַח גָּד֥וֹל לִ⁠י֙ לַ⁠בַּ֔עַל
19.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Since a great sacrifice is to me for Baal, let not a man be missing]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. As the word **servants** indicates, Jehu is speaking specifically of men and women who worship Baal. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women and reflects his meaning. Alternate translation: [anyone who worships Baal]

Here the masculine term **a man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a person] or [anyone]

20.note: Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And his servants proclaimed that there would be an assembly] or [And an assembly was announced]

21.note: Here the masculine term **a man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a person]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:18. Alternate translation: [the temple of Baal]

The expression **was filled** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they filled the house of Baal]

The author is using the term **mouth** to mean “end” or “side.” If this term does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [from end to end] or [to capacity]

22.note: In this context, the word **vestment** refers to a special ceremonial garment that priests and worshipers of Baal wore during religious rituals. These garments signified devotion to Baal and added solemnity to the rituals. If your readers would not be familiar with this type of **vestment**, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the ceremonial garment that signified devotion to Baal]

24.note: The pronoun **they** refers to Jehu and Jehonadab. (The author is probably referring to how they **came in** to the part of the temple where the altar was.) It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And Jehu and Jehonadab came in]

24.q: וְ⁠יֵה֞וּא שָׂם־ל֤⁠וֹ בַ⁠חוּץ֙ שְׁמֹנִ֣ים אִ֔ישׁ וַ⁠יֹּ֗אמֶר הָ⁠אִ֤ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִמָּלֵט֙ מִן־הָ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֤ר אֲנִי֙ מֵבִ֣יא עַל־יְדֵי⁠כֶ֔ם נַפְשׁ֖⁠וֹ תַּ֥חַת נַפְשֽׁ⁠וֹ
24.note: The author is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Jehu was using **his life in place of his life** as a common expression of his culture to mean that any of the men he was stationing outside would forfeit his own life if he allowed any of the **men** from inside the temple to escape. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Kings 20:39. Alternate translation: [the one of you who lets him escape will pay for that with his life] or [we will execute the one of you who lets him get away]

25.note: The author is using the phrase **And it happened** to introduce a new development in this event. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new development.

The term **runners** originally described men who were royal bodyguards and who ran in front of and alongside the king’s chariot to protect him. The term later also described palace guards, as 1 Kings 14:27–28 shows. If you have already translated the book of 1 Kings, see how you translated the term there. Alternate translation: [to the royal guards] or [to the palace guards]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:23. Alternate translation: [kill them]

The author is using as a common expression of his culture to mean that the runners and captains completely destroyed the worshipers of Baal, leaving no survivors. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. If you have already translated the book of 1 Samuel, see how you translated the similar expression in 1 Samuel 22:19. Alternate translation: [And they destroyed them completely]

This could mean: (1) that the runners and captains **threw** the dead bodies of the Baal worshipers out of the temple. Alternate translation: [and the runners and the captains threw their bodies out of the temple] or (2) that the runners and captains **threw** the bodies of the people they killed to one side so that they could continue going through the crowd and killing others. Alternate translation: [and the runners and captains threw to one side the body of each person they killed until they had killed everyone]

In this context, the term **city** seems to describe an inner sanctuary of the temple of Baal where the sacred “pillars” described in the next verse were kept. Alternate translation: [the inner sanctuary of the temple of Baal]

26.note: Since the pronoun **it** refers back to the **pillars** (sacred images) that were kept in the temple of Baal, it may be more natural in your language to use a plural pronoun. Alternate translation: [and they burned them]

27.note: See how you translated the same expression in 2:22.

29.note: To translate the expression **did not turn away** here and in verse 31, see how you translated the similar expression in 3:3. Alternate translation: [Jehu did not stop committing them]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the worship of the calves of gold]

30.q: יַ֤עַן אֲשֶׁר־הֱטִיבֹ֨תָ֙ לַ⁠עֲשׂ֤וֹת הַ⁠יָּשָׁר֙ בְּ⁠עֵינַ֔⁠י כְּ⁠כֹל֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בִּ⁠לְבָבִ֔⁠י עָשִׂ֖יתָ לְ⁠בֵ֣ית אַחְאָ֑ב בְּנֵ֣י רְבִעִ֔ים יֵשְׁב֥וּ לְ⁠ךָ֖ עַל־כִּסֵּ֥א יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
30.note: If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the description of what Jehu did before the information about what Yahweh will do as a result. Alternate translation: [According to all that was in my heart, you did to the house of Ahab. Because you did well by doing right in my eyes, sons of the fourth will sit for you on the throne of Israel]
Here the **heart** represents a person’s desires. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [according to everything that I wanted]
See how you translated the similar expression in [8:1](ta:08). Alternate translation: [to the family of Ahab]

Yahweh is using **sons of the fourth** as a common expression of this culture to mean “four generations of your descendants.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [four generations of your descendants]

Here, sitting on the **throne of Israel** represents ruling Israel as king. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will succeed you as the king of Israel]

31.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 8:18. Alternate translation: [to live according to the law of Yahweh]
Here the **heart** represents a person’s motives and desires. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in complete devotion]

32.note: The author is speaking as if Yahweh had actually **cut off** parts of Israel. He means that Yahweh allowed Hazael to conquer parts of Israel’s territory. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to reduce the territory of Israel]
See how you translated the similar expression in 3:24. Alternate translation: [And Hazael defeated them]

Here the **border** of Israel represents its territory. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [throughout the territory of Israel]

33.note: The author is describing the location of a place in the way that is characteristic of his culture. He means here that if someone were traveling from the territories he is about to describe to the area where most of the Israelites lived, he would be coming **from the rising of the sun**, that is, from the east. In your translation, express this in the way your culture describes the location of places. If you have already translated the book of Joshua, see how you translated the similar expression in Joshua 12:1. Alternate translation: [to the east of the Jordan River]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the land of the Gadite and the Reubenite and the Manassite]

The author is not referring to a specific **Gadite**, **Reubenite**, or **Manassite**. He means members of those tribes in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [the Gadites and the Reubenites and the Manassites]

The author means that in addition to capturing **Aroer**, Hazael conquered territory throughout Gilead all the way to **Bashan**. If that is not clear, you may want to use different connecting words to show how the phrase **and Gilead and Bashan** relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [and throughout Gilead all the way to Bashan]

34.q: וְ⁠יֶ֨תֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י יֵה֛וּא וְ⁠כָל־אֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָׂ֖ה וְ⁠כָל־גְּבוּרָת֑⁠וֹ הֲ⁠לֽוֹא־הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל־סֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַ⁠יָּמִ֖ים לְ⁠מַלְכֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
34.note: In this verse and the next two verses, the author is concluding the story of Jehu. To translate this verse, see how you have translated the comparable phrases in 1:18 and similar contexts in the book.

35.note: See how you translated the same expression in 8:24. Alternate translation: [And Jehu passed away] or [And Jehu died]

Here the author is using the pronoun **they** in a general sense, not to refer to specific people. Use an expression for this that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and people buried him] or [and he was buried]

36.note: Here, **days** represent “time,” since time is made up of days. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And the time … was 28 years]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information that Jehu ruled **in Samaria** with the information that he **was king over Israel**. Alternate translation: [had reigned over Israel in Samaria were 28 years]
